newsitem.title: POLAND: Zloty softens as foreigners sell Polish T-bills.
newsitem.headline: Zloty softens as foreigners sell Polish T-bills.

text.p: The zloty lost some ground against the currency basket after the central bank signalled that the monthly devaluation factor for the Polish currency would remain at one percent per month until the end of 1997.

They said the news caused foreign investors to sell an estimated 80 million zlotys worth of Polish treasuries on the seconary T-bill market, which created additional demand for currencies on the forex market and depressed the zloty.
"The reaction of foreigners may have been nervous, but they did it anyway. It was visible on the forex and the secondary T-bill market," said Jaroslaw Dryjski from Bank Slaski SA.
The zloty closed at 1.79/1.74 pct from the trading band centre against Wednesday's 1.87/83 percent from parity.
It was at 2.8315/30 to the dollar, down from 2.8290/00 on Wednesday and at 1.8398/05 per mark, also down from 1.8360/65.
Dealers said the central bank's statement effectively curbed short-term inflows into Polish treasuries as it capped the interest rate differential expected by foreigners.
"A steady crawling peg may freeze foreign short-term speculation on Polish treasuries," said Krzysztof Kozuchowski, dealer at ING Bank in Warsaw.
In secondary trade, T-bill yields rose on growing supply caused by the foreign withdrawl as well as domestic banks seeking funds after the money market suddenly tightened this morning, dealers said.

The benchmark 52-week T-bill inched up to 19.45 percent, from 19.40 this morning and a 19.43 percent average yield at last Monday's primary tender. Half-year paper was quoted 0.04 point up at 19.17/19.13 percent against Monday's 19.11 percent.
Overnight deposit rates rose to 19.00/19.10 percent from 18.35/18.55 at 0630 GMT. Tomorrow/next were at 18.85/19.50 percent, up from this morning's 18.30/18.55 percent.
The central bank refrained from draining the market, which dealers said signalled that banks were strained ahead of tax-payments around October 20.

But many were were bewildered about the sudden loss of liquidity on Thursday. "It's very strange, money disappeared and rates rose a half a point without an appearent reason," said one dealer in Warsaw.
